Innocent
ĭn´no-cent
adj. (free from guilt in a particular matter; rendering Hebrew naqi, Greek athoos)
From Latin in-, not, and nocens, harming — literally not hurting. Scripture uses it forensically: innocent of a charge, not innocent by nature.

Biblical Definition

Innocent in the Authorized Version is a courtroom word, not a statement about human nature. No son of Adam is innocent before God; but a man may be entirely innocent of the particular crime laid against him, and Scripture guards that innocence with extraordinary severity. The law forbids the judicial murder of the innocent outright — “the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked” (Exo 23:7) — and pronounces a covenant curse on the man who takes a bribe to do it (Deu 27:25). The shedding of innocent blood becomes the standing measure of a nation's apostasy: Manasseh filled Jerusalem with it, and of that particular sin it is written that the LORD “would not pardon” (2Ki 24:4). Jonathan pleads David's case in exactly these terms (1Sa 19:5). The word therefore does double duty in the canon: it protects the wrongly accused, and it convicts the nation that spills their blood.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines innocent as free from guilt, not having done wrong or violated any law, and secondarily as harmless, doing no injury — noting its legal use for one not chargeable with the crime alleged.

expand to see more

IN´NOCENT, a. Not guilty; free from guilt; not having done wrong or violated any law.

2. Free from the guilt of a particular crime or evil action.

3. Unhurtful; harmless in effects.

4. Lawful; permitted; as an innocent trade.

Key Scripture

Exo 23:7 — "Keep thee far from a false matter; and the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked."

Deu 27:25 — "Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. And all the people shall say, Amen."

2Ki 24:4 — "And also for the innocent blood that he shed: for he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood; which the LORD would not pardon."

1Sa 19:5 — "For he did put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine, and the LORD wrought a great salvation for all Israel: thou sawest it, and didst rejoice: wherefore then wilt thou sin against innocent blood, to slay David without a cause?"

Modern Corruption

Innocence relocated from the courtroom to human nature itself — man declared innocent by default — while the actual biblical concern, the shedding of innocent blood, is renamed and defended.

expand to see more

Modern moral vocabulary treats innocence as the natural human condition, corrupted only later by circumstance or society. Scripture reverses the order entirely: men are guilty in Adam and may be innocent only of specific charges. That inversion has consequences at both ends. It removes the need for atonement, since the innocent require no ransom; and it makes conviction of sin feel like an injury done to a person rather than the truth told about him.

Meanwhile the concrete thing Scripture guards — innocent blood — is the very thing the age has learned to justify. The prophets measure a civilization by what it does to those who cannot defend themselves, and 2 Kings 24:4 records a sin of which it is said the LORD would not pardon it. Deuteronomy 27:25 puts a curse on taking payment to destroy an innocent person, and the whole congregation is required to say Amen to it. A nation that has grown comfortable with that transaction is not enlightened; it is under the twenty-seventh chapter of Deuteronomy.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew naqi (H5355), clean, free, acquitted — the word for innocent blood; Greek athoos (G121), unpunished, guiltless — Pilate's word as he washed his hands.

expand to see more

Hebrew naqi (H5355) — clean, exempt, acquitted; the standing phrase dam naqi, innocent blood (Deu 19:10).

Hebrew tsaddiq (H6662) — righteous; paired with innocent in Exo 23:7, showing the forensic register of both.

Greek athoos (G121) — guiltless, unpunished; used by Pilate of himself concerning the blood of the only truly innocent Man.

Usage

"“The innocent and righteous slay thou not” — the law's absolute guard on judicial murder."

"“Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person” — and all the people said, Amen."

"“He filled Jerusalem with innocent blood; which the LORD would not pardon” — the measure of a nation's apostasy."
